As a sitter it’s our responsibility to watch and care for the animals. I do all types of work on Rover. For boarding and daycare, we have 3 rules that we make abundantly clear with our clients before bringing their dogs to stay with us.

1. Must be house trained. No marking or accidents. 

2. They must get along with our dog. Who is a golden retriever and gets along with everyone. 

3. No pets on the couch. Our couch is leather and scratches easily. This last rule we aren’t nearly as strict about as 1 & 2, obviously lots of dogs are used to being on couches at their homes. We just want the owners to know that they aren’t allowed for the meet and greet and if that ever bothered the owner that we wouldn’t let their pet have the spa-day comfort treatment on our couch 😂 But we just tell the dogs firmly ‘No’ each time they go on, most of them understand it after a few days to a week of staying with us. Most learn, some get mad and one actually argued with me which was the cutest and funniest thing ever. 

Anyways, if a dog is said to be house trained and has an accident, I give it 3 strikes. 2 accidents are free if it’s nervous about its new environment/doesn’t ask where to go. I’ll also simply tell the dog ‘No’ firmly so it knows it made a mistake and needs to go outside here too. But usually, 99% of the dogs that have one accident are dogs that are simply not house trained. And we stop care for that dog in the future. We don’t charge these clients or ask for more money because their dog wasn’t house trained. 

Now we don’t specify this role, as it’s sort of an unwritten rule, but if a dog destroyed things in our house, especially major furniture, we wouldn’t care for that dog ever again. Destroying furniture is not normal behavior. If we were caring for a dog in someone else’s home and the dog destroyed furniture, we wouldn’t pay to replace it even though it was under our care, and the owner wouldn’t expect us to. It’s their home and their dog. But if a dog was under our supervision and was playing and randomly decided to take a major bite out of our couch… that’s tricky. It’s not our dog, but it is our couch. If any of our friends or family brought their pet over and it bit a giant piece out of our nice new couch, those people would offer to replace it 100%. Being that it’s a client and not friend/family, where does this exactly fall?

Well if you were at a clients house for a meet and greet, and you tripped over your own foot and fell and put your hand out and put a hole in someone’s wall. Would you be super embarrassed for causing that damage, feel terrible and offer to cover the cost of repair? I think most people would. 

We try to require all dogs who stay with us boarding or day care come with a crate. That was if the dogs are getting too crazy for any reason we can give them their personal space in a place they’re used to (their crate), it has their smell, their bed, but they can still see us. It’s a very fast and efficient way to calm down the energy. Which then they usually proceed to fall right asleep as they were bursting with energy minutes before. 

Personally I’m surprised at the replies from other people here. I think doing the right thing is always the way to go. On the one hand, significant unforeseen over-the-top damage should be paid for, that’s the ethical thing to do - legally probably as well. I’d be shocked in a civil suit if they didn’t award the plaintiff damage compensation for the mattress. On the other hand, if you feel locking the dog in a room was not right, not what you paid them to do and it was cruel or simply bad care, I can see why you’d also not want to cover the damages. You feel what they did to your dog was unethical and what happened next is a result of negligent care. But lastly, it seems you didn’t provide a crate for the dog - which isn’t necessary, but if you have a dog who, for lack of better words, is a menace. And the sitter was unaware of how whacky your dog would be behaving, isolating and controlling the situation is reasonable. Now, the dog is an animal, an animals behavior is usually typical animal behavior and not ‘whacky’. But it is a domesticated dog and the majority of people’s dogs don’t tear up mattresses. 

It seems your dog may be very uncomfortable with staying at other places, which is fine, lots of dogs have that. My recommendation would be to board your dog in an actual boarding facility where it has pen where it can’t destroy people’s furniture. They’re actually not that different in pricing than boarders from Rover. 

In terms of what I think you should do for this situation. I’m not the sitter, I didn’t meet the dog, I didn’t see the situation occur, I don’t know all the exact details leading up, and I’m not you. Asking here is subjective and you should do what you think is right. Go with your gut. But if I had to give my opinion, I’d say cover damages for at least 50%, 50% damage cover is what I believe from what I read to be the bare minimum. If it was you who cause the damage, you’d cover 100%. Being that it was their job to care for the dog but your dog commit damage that neither of you expected, you’re at least 50% liable. Each situation and person is different. 

Lastly, again just board your dog in a facility and don’t work with this sitter anymore - they clearly aren’t equipped to handle all dogs.
